name: Back Take from Ashi
description: Master Back Take from Ashi Garami in BJJ. Step-by-step transition from leg entanglement to back control. Success rates: Beginner 30%, Intermediate 50%, Advanced 65%.
overview:
The Back Take from Ashi Garami represents a critical strategic pivot in the modern leg lock game, allowing practitioners to convert leg entanglement control into the most dominant position in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu. When an opponent successfully defends leg attacks by hiding their heel or creates defensive frames that prevent submission finishes, the back take offers an alternative path to victory that maintains offensive momentum rather than resetting to neutral positions.

This transition exploits a fundamental vulnerability in leg lock defense: when opponents sit up aggressively to address leg attacks or attempt to extract their trapped leg, they often expose their back. The technique requires recognizing the precise moment when opponent commits their weight forward and redirecting their momentum to facilitate the transition. Rather than forcing submissions against strong defense, the back take follows the principle of flowing to the path of least resistance while maintaining constant threat.

The back take from ashi has become increasingly important in modern competition as leg lock defenses have improved. High-level practitioners use the threat of leg attacks to create back take opportunities, and the threat of back takes to create leg lock openings. This creates a systematic dilemma where defending one attack opens vulnerability to the other, embodying the interconnected nature of positional grappling at advanced levels.
key_principles: Recognize when opponent's defensive posture creates back exposure by sitting up or reaching toward you
Maintain control of trapped leg throughout transition to prevent complete escape and preserve attacking options
Use opponent's forward momentum against them by redirecting rather than resisting their defensive movement
Establish upper body control before releasing leg control to ensure seamless transition to back position
Create angle toward opponent's back before initiating transition rather than moving directly behind
Maintain constant forward pressure during transition to prevent opponent from recovering guard or standing
setup_requirements: Inside Ashi-Garami established with inside leg across opponent's hip and outside leg hooking behind their knee
Opponent sitting up aggressively or reaching forward toward your legs creating back exposure
Opponent's heel defended or rotated away making immediate leg attack submission unlikely
Clear path to opponent's back without obstructions from their defensive frames or grips
Your upper body positioned to reach opponent's torso as you release leg control

execution_steps.description: Identify when opponent sits up to address leg control or reaches forward to create defensive frames, exposing their back as they shift weight toward you.
Before releasing any leg control, reach with your inside arm to secure a grip on opponent's far shoulder, collar, or underhook position to establish upper body control.
Remove your inside leg from across opponent's hip while maintaining outside leg hook, using this leg to push off the mat and begin circling toward their back.
execution_steps.timing: As upper body grip is secured

execution_steps.description: Hip escape and circle your body toward opponent's back, using your outside leg hook as an anchor point while your inside leg swings around to establish first hook behind their hip.
As you arrive at opponent's back, secure seatbelt grip with one arm over their shoulder and other under their armpit, hands clasped together controlling upper body.
Release remaining leg control on opponent's original trapped leg and insert second hook inside their thigh, completing back control with both hooks and seatbelt established.
Pull opponent onto their side or take them down to the mat, establishing chest-to-back connection with full back control including both hooks deep and harness secured.

common_counters.counter: Opponent immediately stands and runs away when they feel leg control release
common_counters.your_response: Maintain grip on their leg or pants as you transition, using their standing motion to pull yourself up to standing back control or immediately shooting for takedown

common_counters.counter: Opponent turns into you and establishes closed guard as you release leg control
common_counters.your_response: Keep your inside leg ready to backstep and prevent guard closure, or accept closed guard top position as still advantageous compared to failed leg lock

common_counters.counter: Opponent sprawls hard and pushes your upper body away preventing back connection
common_counters.your_response: Return to leg entanglement immediately by re-establishing inside ashi control since opponent's sprawl often re-exposes their leg for submission attacks

common_counters.counter: Opponent reaches back and establishes whizzer or overhook preventing hook insertion
common_counters.your_response: Use body lock or mat return to establish control despite whizzer, or transition to truck position using their overhook as a lever point

common_errors.error: Releasing leg control before establishing upper body grip on opponent
common_errors.consequence: Opponent escapes completely to standing or guard position, losing all positional advantage gained from leg entanglement
common_errors.correction: Always secure upper body grip with at least one hand before releasing any leg control, ensuring continuous connection throughout transition

common_errors.error: Attempting back take when opponent is not sitting up or reaching forward
common_errors.consequence: Opponent easily defends by maintaining low posture and you lose leg entanglement without gaining back position
common_errors.correction: Only initiate back take when opponent commits weight forward, otherwise continue threatening leg attacks to create the opening

common_errors.error: Moving directly behind opponent instead of circling at an angle
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can easily turn and face you or turtle defensively, preventing clean back control establishment
common_errors.correction: Circle toward opponent's back at an angle, using hip movement to arrive at their side before transitioning fully behind

common_errors.error: Failing to insert hooks quickly after arriving at back position
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can turn out, stand up, or escape before back control is consolidated, wasting the successful transition
common_errors.correction: Prioritize hook insertion immediately upon arriving at back, even before perfecting seatbelt grip

common_errors.error: Losing chest-to-back connection during transition allowing space
common_errors.consequence: Opponent creates frames or turns to face you, converting your back take attempt into guard recovery
common_errors.correction: Maintain constant forward pressure and chest connection throughout transition, staying heavy on opponent's back

training_progressions.description: Practice the transition sequence without resistance, focusing on the order of operations: recognize trigger, secure upper body, release inside leg, circle, establish hooks. Drill 50 repetitions per side per session.

Partner provides light resistance and varies timing of sitting up or reaching forward. Practice recognizing the trigger and initiating transition at correct moment. Include failed attempts where timing is wrong.
Combine back take with leg attack threats, flowing between ankle lock attempts, heel hook threats, and back take based on partner's defensive reactions. Practice reading which option is available.
Apply technique in positional sparring starting from inside ashi. Both partners work at full resistance with goal of either completing leg lock, taking back, or escaping. Track success rate.

variants_and_adaptations.variant_name: Kiss of the Dragon back take
variants_and_adaptations.description: When opponent stands from ashi, use your outside leg to hook their far leg while inverting underneath them, spinning to their back as they attempt to pass. Higher risk but effective against standing opponents.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When opponent stands up explosively and you maintain leg hook connection

variants_and_adaptations.description: Instead of releasing leg control immediately, transition through crab ride position by keeping outside leg hook while circling behind opponent, using your shin across their hip as a lever point for back access.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When opponent is on all fours or turtled with you maintaining leg control

variants_and_adaptations.description: Release leg control and immediately sit to opponent's hip on the side away from their trapped leg, establishing back control from a seated position before they can turn to face you.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When opponent is heavily committed to removing your leg control and creates significant forward pressure

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the primary goal of Back Take from Ashi?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The primary goal is to convert a leg entanglement position into back control when leg attack submissions are being effectively defended. This allows maintaining offensive pressure rather than resetting to neutral positions, and creates a systematic dilemma where defending leg attacks exposes the back.

knowledge_assessment.question: What position do you start Back Take from Ashi from?
knowledge_assessment.answer: This technique starts from Inside Ashi-Garami with you in the top/controlling position. You must have your inside leg across opponent's hip and outside leg hooking behind their knee, with established control of their trapped leg.

knowledge_assessment.question: What are the key grips needed for Back Take from Ashi?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Initially you need whatever grip controls the trapped leg in ashi. Before transitioning, you must secure upper body connection with at least one arm reaching to opponent's far shoulder, collar, or establishing underhook. Final grips are seatbelt configuration with one arm over shoulder and one under armpit.

knowledge_assessment.question: Your opponent is defending your heel hook by keeping their knee rotated away - when should you transition to back take versus continuing to attack the leg?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Transition to back take when opponent sits up aggressively to address your leg control or reaches forward creating back exposure. If they maintain low defensive posture without sitting up, continue leg attack threats to force the reaction. The back take requires forward commitment from opponent - without this trigger, forcing the transition loses both positions.

knowledge_assessment.question: How do you counter Back Take from Ashi?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Primary counters include maintaining low defensive posture without sitting up, immediately turning into the attacker to establish guard when leg control releases, standing and creating distance before back control is established, or establishing whizzer/overhook to prevent hook insertion. The key is recognizing the transition attempt early and not committing weight forward.

knowledge_assessment.question: When is the best time to attempt Back Take from Ashi?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The optimal timing is when opponent sits up to address your leg control, reaches forward to strip grips, or commits weight toward you while defending heel exposure. This forward commitment creates the back exposure necessary for clean transition. Attempting when opponent maintains low defensive posture typically fails.

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the correct sequence for releasing leg control during the transition?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Always secure upper body grip first before releasing any leg control. Then release your inside leg while maintaining outside leg hook as an anchor. Use the inside leg to push off the mat and circle toward opponent's back. Only release the outside leg hook after first back hook is inserted and seatbelt is established. This sequencing ensures continuous control throughout.

knowledge_assessment.question: Your opponent stands up explosively as you initiate the back take - how do you adjust?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Maintain any grip on their leg or pants and use their standing motion to pull yourself up to standing back control, or immediately shoot for single leg takedown since their base is compromised. Alternatively, if you have good outside leg connection, consider inverting for Kiss of the Dragon entry. Do not try to pull them back down - use their momentum rather than fighting it.

safety_considerations: This transition involves releasing leg control and moving dynamically to opponent's back, which carries lower injury risk than most leg lock positions but requires controlled practice. Primary safety concerns include avoiding explosive movements that could torque opponent's knee as you release leg control, and ensuring controlled descent when taking opponent to mat from back position. Practice initially at slow speed to develop the timing and pathway. When drilling with resistance, communicate clearly about intensity levels. The transition itself does not apply joint stress but careless execution during release of leg control could strain opponent's knee if their leg is still entangled during explosive movement.
position_integration: The Back Take from Ashi represents a critical branch point in the modern leg lock system, connecting leg entanglements to the back control submission system. This technique embodies the principle of position over submission - when leg attacks are defended, converting to the most dominant position maintains offensive pressure. The transition integrates with the broader ashi garami system as an alternative outcome when opponents successfully defend heel exposure, creating a systematic dilemma: defend the heel and expose the back, or maintain back safety and allow leg attack progression. This technique chains naturally with back control submissions including rear naked choke, armbar from back, and bow and arrow choke. It also works in reverse - the threat of back take forces opponents to address upper body control, which can re-expose their heel for leg attacks.
